thread:
mira: Heads-up — I'm trying to capture a ~2min run of our batching experiment to inspect kernel selection + KV-cache stalls. Want to record kernel timelines, NVTX markers, and OS runtime events but avoid massive traces. Any recommended nsys CLI flags? :mag:

sam: Use trace=cuda,nvtx,osrt so you get kernel timeline + our NVTX spans + OS threads. Limit duration and PID to keep file small. Example I use:```
nsys profile --trace=cuda,nvtx,osrt --sample=cpu --duration=120 --output=nsys_bench --capture-range=nvtx --force-overwrite --pid=12345```
Change --duration and --pid as needed.

jordan: minor tweak: I prefer --sample=none for short runs where we only need event timelines (kernel & nvtx) — sampling adds overhead & file size. If you want CPU stack samples use --sample=cpu with a reasonable interval. Also consider --capture-range=nsys:start,stop if you instrument start/stop.

mira: Good call. We do want a few CPU samples around the batching hotpaths though to confirm threads spinning on KV cache lock. Maybe 1s duration for warmup then capture 60s of steady-state. How to do warmup capture without blowing up files?

sam: Warmup approach: run once w/o profiling, then start profiling with --delay=60 (or sleep in wrapper) so nsys only records steady-state. Or use our NVTX markers: emit NVTX("warmup_end") and profile with --capture-range=nvtx to start recording on that marker. Example wrapper:```
sleep 60 &
nsys profile --trace=cuda,nvtx,osrt --sample=cpu --duration=60 --output=steady_run --pid=$PID```
That keeps the qdrep small.

jordan: For PID filtering: if your process forks worker processes the main PID might miss GPU work — use --processes=$(pgrep -f serving_runtime) or omit pid and post-filter by process name in the UI. Also the --trace-filter option can reduce noise (exclude driver or unrelated libraries).

mira: Any tips for kernel selection analysis? I want to see when we pick quantized kernels vs fallback FP ones; NVTX markers are in place around compile/select calls but not every kernel.

sam: NVTX around model dispatch is great. In the timeline: look for kernel names like aten::* or cutlass kernels; long kernels preceded by small memcpy or kCache hits often signal cache misses. Use the Summary -> CUDA API / Kernel table and sort by start time and duration. Also enable "Show source" in the timeline to inspect NVTX labels.

jordan: If you suspect KV cache stalls, record host-side stacks: --sample=cpu with --sample-interval=100us (or default) will show spinning threads on futex/lock. Then in the sampling flame you can see which function holds the lock.

mira: Ok will try:```
# warmup first, then start profiling on NVTX marker for 90s with light CPU sampling
nsys profile --trace=cuda,nvtx,osrt --sample=cpu --sample-interval=100us --capture-range=nvtx --duration=90 -o /tmp/nsys/kv_bench --force-overwrite
```
Is output .qdrep -> .sqlite for timeline? I usually open .qdrep in UI and export .sqlite for script parsing.

sam: yep .qdrep is native, UI -> export -> sqlite works for programmatic queries. Also use `nsys stats -r cuda -o summary.txt /tmp/nsys/kv_bench.qdrep` for quick text stats.

ops-bot: deploy-bot: started a background capture on runner-12 (pid=8912) at 1765432130 :robot_face:

mira: Thanks — I ran it and saw a long burst of kernels labelled cutlass_gemm_int8 then a 30ms CPU gap where threads were in spin loop. Will parse sqlite and share a short timeline screenshot. :camera_flash:

jordan: Nice. If you paste the timeline qdrep I can triage kernel vs host interaction. Also consider using --trace=osrt for fine-grained OS runtime events if you suspect scheduler preemption (we already added osrt above).

mira: Will do. Sharing qdrep in #perf-artifacts when ready. Cheers! :tada:
